beginner.headline: Collins Chooses Mogging as Its Word of the Year
beginner.brief: Collins English Dictionary chose mogging as its word of the year. Mogging means doing better than someone or getting more attention than them. People often use this word to talk about how someone looks. It became much more common in 2026. Young people use it online and in everyday conversation. It can be a joke about someone or a way to say something nice about them. How people understand it can change with the situation. Collins uses social media to learn how English is changing. Its dictionary team checks how often people use words.

intermediate.headline: Mogging Becomes Collins' Word of the Year
intermediate.brief: Mogging has been named word of the year by the Collins English Dictionary. The informal term describes outshining someone, especially by looking more attractive than they do. It is popular with Generations Z and Alpha, both online and in everyday conversation. Its usage increased by 210% as it became mainstream in 2026. Depending on the context, people can use it as either a compliment or a playful put-down. Collins' managing director Alex Beecroft explained that language experts study how often words appear and examine patterns in their use. He said the selection shows how each generation influences language. Collins uses a range of sources, including social media, to follow changes in English in the UK. The shortlist also included ghost job, an advertised position that an employer has no intention of filling. In 2025, Collins selected vibe coding, which means creating an app or website by describing it to artificial intelligence.

advanced.headline: Collins Names Mogging Its Word of the Year
advanced.brief: Collins English Dictionary has named mogging its word of the year. Used playfully, the expression describes outperforming or upstaging another person or thing. The term gained currency beyond its younger users in 2026, when its use rose by 210%, having spread among Generations Z and Alpha both online and in everyday speech. Collins managing director Alex Beecroft says lexicographers, specialists who research words for dictionaries, examine how frequently expressions occur. They also analyse recurring contexts to identify linguistic trends, or broader developments in how people use language. Beecroft interprets the choice as evidence that successive generations leave their mark on language. Mogging is often traced back to AMOG, an acronym formed from Alpha Male of the Group. The term has also been associated with bodybuilding forums in the mid-2010s. Far from being invariably insulting, the term can function as either a playful put-down or a compliment, depending on context. Its comparative meaning most often concerns physical appearance, with one person appearing more impressive than another. It circulates in looks maxxing communities, online groups whose members exchange advice on maximising their physical attractiveness. To reflect changes in English in the United Kingdom, Collins draws on varied material, including social media. Its 2025 choice was vibe coding, the practice of creating an app or website by describing it to artificial intelligence rather than manually writing programming code. Another expression on this year’s ten-item list is ghost job, referring to a position advertised by an employer with no intention of appointing anyone.
